citations.quote:
Throughout this page, assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]): the
analytic and cohomological suppliers invoked by the results below assume full
AC, and each item records its exact use. The definitional content below uses no
choice.

**(1) Compact Kähler manifolds.** Let $n\ge1$. A **Kähler manifold** is a complex
manifold $X$ of complex dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]) with complex structure
$J$ and a **Hermitian metric** $g$ — a Riemannian metric
([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) satisfying
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all tangent vectors $v,w$ — whose **real fundamental form**
$\omega(v,w)=g(Jv,w)$ is

- a smooth real 2-form, the section of $\Lambda^2T^*X$ obtained by alternating
  $g(J\cdot,\cdot)$;
- **positive**: $\omega(v,Jv)=g(Jv,Jv)>0$ for every nonzero tangent vector $v$;
- **closed**: $d\omega=0$.

The manifold is **compact Kähler** when the topological space $X$ is compact.

**Orientation.** For a complex basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of a tangent space $T_xX$,
the ordered real basis $(v_1,Jv_1,\dots,v_n,Jv_n)$ is declared **positive**. This
is well defined: two complex bases differ by a complex-linear automorphism, whose
real determinant is the square of the modulus of its complex determinant and so
is positive, and the local orientations therefore glue along holomorphic charts
to a global orientation of $X$. Let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be a $g$-orthonormal complex
frame, so $g(v_j,v_k)=\delta_{jk}$ and $g(v_j,Jv_k)=0$, and let $e_j=g(v_j,\cdot)$ and
$f_j=g(Jv_j,\cdot)$ be the metric-dual covectors. Then
$(e_1,f_1,\dots,e_n,f_n)$ is a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe,
$f_j=-Je_j$ for the pullback action $(J\alpha)(v)=\alpha(Jv)$ of $J$ on
covectors, and

$$\omega=\sum_{j=1}^n e_j\wedge f_j .$$

The **oriented volume form** is the top form

$$dV:=\frac{\omega^n}{n!}=e_1\wedge f_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_n\wedge f_n ,$$

which evaluates to $1$ on each positively oriented $g$-orthonormal frame.

**Complex dimension zero.** For $n=0$ a complex manifold is a discrete space and
compactness makes it a finite set of points with its unique complex structure;
there are no tangent vectors and no forms of positive degree, $\omega=0$, and the
operators $L,\Lambda,\partial,\bar\partial,d,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ and
all Laplacians introduced below are zero. The Hodge star is the identity on
degree zero, and $dV$ is the counting measure.

**(2) Complex-valued forms and Kähler operators.** Let $X$ be compact Kähler.
Write $\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth $k$-forms, the
complex-linear extension of the real forms of
[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]; the Hodge star $*$ of
[[def-riemannian-hodge-star]] extends complex-linearly, and for
$\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ the **integral inner product**

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=\int_X\alpha\wedge*\bar\beta$$

is complex-linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second; the
integral is that of
[[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-top-form-on-an-oriented-manifold]] and
the integrand is $\lvert\alpha\rvert^2\,dV$ when $\beta=\alpha$, so the pairing
is a positive definite Hermitian form. In holomorphic charts

$$\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\Omega^{p,q}(X),\qquad d=\partial+\bar\partial ,$$

with $\partial$ and $\bar\partial$ of bidegree $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$
([[def-bigraded-complex-differential-forms]]); the decomposition is independent
of the holomorphic chart because holomorphic chart changes preserve bidegree.

Put $L=\omega\wedge$, so that $L:\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)\to\Omega^{k+2}(X;\mathbb C)$,
and let $\Lambda,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ be the formal adjoints of
$L,\partial,\bar\partial,d$ with respect to $\langle\,,\rangle$; existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[lem-formal-adjoints-of-differential-operators-exist-and-are-unique]], applied
to the bundle of complex-valued forms with the metric of
[[prop-riemannian-metrics-induce-metrics-on-dual-tensor-and-exterior-bundles]]
and the density $dV$. The **Laplacians** are

$$\Delta_d=dd^*+d^*d,\qquad \Delta_\partial=\partial\partial^*+\partial^*\partial,\qquad \Delta_{\bar\partial}=\bar\partial\bar\partial^*+\bar\partial^*\bar\partial ,$$

and $\epsilon(k)=(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$.

**(3) Rational pure Hodge structures.** Let $k\in\mathbb Z$. A **rational pure
Hodge structure of weight $k$** is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space
$V$ together with a direct-sum decomposition by $\mathbb C$-subspaces

$$V_{\mathbb C}=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}V^{p,q},\qquad \overline{V^{p,q}}=V^{q,p},$$

where conjugation is the $\mathbb C$-antilinear involution
$v\otimes\lambda\mapsto v\otimes\bar\lambda$. The sum is finite because
$V_{\mathbb C}$ is finite dimensional, and it is direct by definition. The **Weil
operator** $C$ is the $\mathbb C$-linear endomorphism of $V_{\mathbb C}$ acting
as $i^{p-q}$ on $V^{p,q}$; the conjugation symmetry makes $C$ commute with
conjugation, so $C$ is the complexification of a real-linear endomorphism
of $V_{\mathbb R}=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$. It need not preserve $V$.

A **polarization** of such a Hodge structure is a nondegenerate $\mathbb Q$-bilinear
form $Q:V\times V\to\mathbb Q$, extended $\mathbb C$-bilinearly to $V_{\mathbb C}$,
such that

- $Q(y,x)=(-1)^kQ(x,y)$ for all $x,y$;
- $Q(V^{p,q},V^{a,b})=0$ unless $(a,b)=(q,p)$;
- $h(x,y)=Q(Cx,\bar y)$ is a positive definite Hermitian form on $V_{\mathbb C}$.

A **rational sub-Hodge structure** is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace
$U\subseteq V$ with $U_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}(U_{\mathbb C}\cap V^{p,q})$.
The **Tate shift** $V(-r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, keeps the underlying $\mathbb Q$-vector
space, the Weil operator and $Q$ as they are and moves the bidegrees to
$(p+r,q+r)$, so that the weight becomes $k+2r$; equivalently, $(V(-r))^{p,q}=V^{p-r,q-r}$.

Let $n\ge0$, let $V$ be a real inner product space of dimension $2n$, and let
$J:V\to V$ be a compatible complex structure ($J^2=-\mathrm{id}$ and
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all $v,w$). Let $\omega\in\bigwedge^2V$ satisfy
$\omega(v,w)=-g(Jv,w)$ for all $v,w$, and orient $V$ so that $\omega^n/n!$ is a
positive volume form. These are the form-side conventions of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]]: $V$ is the
cotangent space at a point, $J$ acts on forms by pullback, and $\omega$ is the
fundamental form. Write $h$ for the induced determinant pairing on the complexified exterior
algebra $\bigwedge^\bullet V_{\mathbb C}$, extended sesquilinearly from $g$
with distinct degrees orthogonal and conjugate-linearity in the second variable, put $L=\omega\wedge$, let $\Lambda=L^*$ be the adjoint
with respect to $h$, and put $H=[L,\Lambda]$ and
$W=\exp L\exp(-\Lambda)\exp L$. Degrees of exterior powers below range over $0\le k\le2n$ (exterior powers
outside this range are zero). Let $J$ also denote the algebra endomorphism
$J(x\wedge y)=Jx\wedge Jy$ of $\bigwedge^\bullet V_{\mathbb C}$, let
$\bigwedge^{p,q}V_{\mathbb C}$ be the span of $p$-fold wedges of
$V^{1,0}=\ker(J-i)$ with $q$-fold wedges of $V^{0,1}=\ker(J+i)$, and let $*$ be
the complex-linear extension of the Hodge star of $V$ and
$\epsilon(k)=(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$.

Then the following hold.

1. $H=[L,\Lambda]$ satisfies $[L,\Lambda]=H$, $H=(k-n)\mathrm{id}$ on
   $\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$, $[H,L]=2L$ and $[H,\Lambda]=-2\Lambda$.
2. Every $\alpha\in\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$ has a unique decomposition
   $\alpha=\sum_{r\ge\max(0,k-n)}L^ru_r$ with $\Lambda u_r=0$ and
   $u_r\in\bigwedge^{k-2r}V_{\mathbb C}$; all but finitely many terms vanish,
   and the projections $\alpha\mapsto u_r$ are rational polynomials in
   $L,\Lambda$ on each fixed degree.
3. If $0\le t\le n$ and $u\in\bigwedge^tV_{\mathbb C}$ is primitive
   ($\Lambda u=0$) of degree $t$,
   then $L^{n-t+1}u=0$ and
   $$\Lambda^sL^ru=\frac{r!}{(r-s)!}\frac{(n-t-r+s)!}{(n-t-r)!}L^{r-s}u\qquad(0\le s\le r\le n-t);$$
   no nonzero primitive element has degree $t>n$; for $k\le n$ an element of
   $\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$ is primitive exactly when $L^{n-k+1}u=0$; and
   $L^{n-k}:\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}\to\bigwedge^{2n-k}V_{\mathbb C}$ is an
   isomorphism for $k\le n$.
4. $J=i^{p-q}$ on $\bigwedge^{p,q}V_{\mathbb C}$, and
   $W\alpha=\epsilon(k)J*\alpha$ for every $\alpha$ of degree $k$. If $0\le k=p+q\le n$ and $u$ is
   primitive of type $(p,q)$, then
   $$*u=\frac{\epsilon(k)i^{q-p}}{(n-k)!}L^{n-k}u .$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
analytic suppliers below. Let $X$ be a compact Kähler $n$-fold with Kähler form
$\omega$, in the conventions of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]], and put
$L=[\omega]\smile(-)$ on cohomology. Then the following hold.

- $L^{n-k}:H^k(X;\mathbb R)\to H^{2n-k}(X;\mathbb R)$ is an isomorphism for
  $0\le k\le n$.
- Harmonic representatives transport $(L,\Lambda,H)$ to an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$
  action: $L$ is cup product with $[\omega]$, $\Lambda$ on cohomology means
  applying $\Lambda$ to the harmonic representative and not to an arbitrary
  closed form, $H$ acts by $\deg-n$, and
  $[L,\Lambda]=H$, $[H,L]=2L$, $[H,\Lambda]=-2\Lambda$ hold on cohomology.
- Primitive cohomology is
  $P^k=\{a\in H^k(X;\mathbb R):\text{the harmonic representative of }a\text{ lies in }\ker\Lambda\}$,
  and for $0\le k\le n$ one has
  $P^k=\ker\bigl(L^{n-k+1}:H^k(X;\mathbb R)\to H^{2n-k+2}(X;\mathbb R)\bigr)$;
  for every $k$,
  $$H^k(X;\mathbb R)=\bigoplus_{r\ge\max(0,k-n)}L^rP^{k-2r},$$
  and a class of type $(p,q)$ has primitive components of type $(p-r,q-r)$.
- If $[\omega]$ is the real image of a rational class
  $\ell\in H^2(X;\mathbb Q)$, all these decompositions and $L$-isomorphisms are
  rational, and they remain isomorphisms after extension to every
  characteristic-zero field.

Assume AC. For a compact Kähler manifold $X$ in the sense of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]], every de
Rham class has a unique smooth harmonic representative and
$$H^k(X;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^{p,q}(X),\qquad \overline{H^{p,q}(X)}=H^{q,p}(X).$$
Here $H^{p,q}(X)$ is precisely the set of classes with a $d$-closed smooth
representative of type $(p,q)$, so the decomposition is independent of the
Kähler metric. Writing $\Omega_X^p$ for the sheaf of holomorphic $p$-forms (the
kernel of $\bar\partial$ on the sheaf $\mathcal A^{p,0}$ of smooth $(p,0)$-forms),
$H^{p,q}(X)$ is isomorphic to $H^q(X,\Omega_X^p)$, the sheaf cohomology of
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]. The Hodge filtration
$F^a=\bigoplus_{p\ge a}H^{p,k-p}$ of $H^k(X;\mathbb C)$ equals the filtration
induced by the holomorphic-degree filtration of the de Rham complex, whose
spectral sequence has $E_1^{p,q}=H^q(X,\Omega_X^p)$ and degenerates at $E_1$.
Pullback by holomorphic maps of compact Kähler manifolds and cup product
preserve Hodge type, so $H^k(X;\mathbb Q)$ is a functorial rational pure Hodge
structure.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth boundaryless
$m$-manifold and let $\alpha\in\Omega^m(M)$ be a smooth real or complex top form.
Let $J_M:H^m_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\to H^m_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R)$ be the de Rham
comparison of [[thm-de-rham-theorem]] for real forms, extended
complex-linearly with codomain $H^m_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb C)$ for complex
forms. Use the smooth-orientation normalization: a positively oriented affine
$m$-simplex represents the positive local homology generator at each interior
point. Let $[M]\in H_m(M;\mathbb R)$ be the real fundamental class of
[[def-fundamental-class-of-a-compact-oriented-manifold]], and let
$\langle\,,\rangle$ be the Kronecker evaluation pairing
([[def-kronecker-evaluation-pairing]]). Then

$$\langle J_M[\alpha],[M]\rangle=\int_M\alpha .$$

Consequently, if $c_1,\dots,c_r\in H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)$ with
$\sum_i\deg c_i=m$ are represented by closed smooth forms $\alpha_i$, then

$$\langle J_M(c_1)\smile\cdots\smile J_M(c_r),[M]\rangle=\int_M\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_r .$$

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold with boundary, $n\geq1$, and let $\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(M)$. With $j:\partial M\hookrightarrow M$ and the outward-normal-first orientation,
$$\int_M d\eta=\int_{\partial M}j^*\eta.$$
An empty boundary contributes zero; in dimension one its integral is a finite signed sum of point values.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional Hausdorff
second-countable smooth manifold, possibly with boundary or empty, and let
$L\to M$ be a smooth complex line bundle with a supplied Hermitian metric and
Hermitian connection $\nabla$. Write $\Omega_\nabla$ for its curvature and
$c_1(L):=e(L_{\mathbb R})$ for the published integral line class, using the
complex orientation on the underlying real plane. Let
$$\rho_M:H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H^2(M;\mathbb R)$$
be induced by $\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$. Under the natural de Rham
isomorphism $J_M$,
$$J_M\left[ -\frac{\Omega_\nabla}{2\pi i}\right]=\rho_M(c_1(L)).$$
For a disconnected base the same line-class convention is understood on each
component; the global class is the Euler class displayed above.

If $\nabla'$ is any complex connection on $L$, not necessarily metric
compatible, then
$$\left[-\frac{\Omega_{\nabla'}}{2\pi i}\right]=\iota_M\!\left(J_M^{-1}\rho_M(c_1(L))\right)\quad\text{in }H^2_{\rm dR}(M;\mathbb C),$$
where $\iota_M$ is induced by including real-valued forms into complex-valued
forms. Thus the arbitrary-connection class is identified with the same real
class by the degree-one transgression.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
Jacobian-criterion, ample-powers, Chern-form and comparison suppliers below.
Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex scheme of pure dimension $n\ge0$.

Then the closed points of $X$ carry a structure of **complex manifold**
$X^{\mathrm{an}}$, its **analytification**: if $X\ne\varnothing$ and $n\ge1$
this is a compact Hausdorff second-countable smooth complex manifold of complex
dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]); if $n=0$ it is the
finite discrete set $X(\mathbb C)$ with its unique complex structure in the
convention of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]]; and if
$X=\varnothing$ then $X^{\mathrm{an}}=\varnothing$. Every standard smooth
algebraic chart of $X$ becomes a holomorphic chart of $X^{\mathrm{an}}$, and
more generally, every morphism between smooth separated finite-type complex schemes of pure dimensions induces a holomorphic map between their analytifications. These analytifications are constructed by the same charts and need not be compact; separatedness and finite type ensure that they are Hausdorff and second-countable.

Moreover, for every ample invertible sheaf $A$ on $X$ there is a smooth
positive closed real $(1,1)$-form $\eta_A$ on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$ whose de Rham
class is the real image of the topological first Chern class
$c_1(A):=c_1(A^{\mathrm{an}})\in H^2(X^{\mathrm{an}};\mathbb Z)$:
$$J_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}[\eta_A]=\rho_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}\bigl(c_1(A)\bigr),$$
where $J$ is the de Rham comparison and $\rho$ the change of coefficients
$\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$
([[lem-rational-cohomology-scalar-comparison-for-compact-smooth-manifolds]]).
In dimension $n=0$ and for $X=\varnothing$ every $2$-form and every degree-two
cohomology class is zero and $\eta_A=0$, so the identity holds trivially.

Assume AC. For a compact smooth manifold $X$, the natural coefficient maps
induce isomorphisms $H^k(X;\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}F\cong H^k(X;F)$ for
every characteristic-zero field $F$, finite-dimensional in each degree. For
$F=\mathbb R,\mathbb C$ these identify singular cohomology with the real or
complex de Rham cohomology. They preserve cup products and are natural for maps
between such manifolds. No ordered-field or positivity structure is asserted
for a general $F$.

The zero class has $Q_k(0,b)=0$ in step 1.1, and the cases $k=0$ with $(n-0)!$ and the $r=0$ summand are included there and in step 3.1.
The one-dimensional endpoint cases $k=0$ and $k=n$ are the factorial and $\epsilon(n)$ evaluations of step 1.1, with the rank-zero case $k<2$ in step 5.1.

Zero primitive spaces have vacuous positivity; the zero Kähler form occurs in complex dimension zero only, where degree-zero evaluation is the positive sum over the finite point set. No zero class is assumed Kähler in positive dimension.
The degree endpoints $k=0$ and $k=n$ are computed in step 1.1, and degrees $k>n$ are handled by the transport of step 3.1.
The general Stokes theorem assumes only $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, derived from the standing AC by the choice chain in step 1.1; no other selection occurs apart from the declared suppliers.

Weil on the conjugate primitive harmonic form gives i^(p-q)Q_k(a,bar a)=(n-k)! norm(a)^2; distinct types then give a positive Hermitian form and nondegeneracy. Cross strings vanish because r<s puts at least n-(k-2r)+1 L factors on the harmonic primitive a_r; (-1)^r epsilon(k)=epsilon(k-2r) makes the block forms positive. Throughout this page, assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]): the
analytic and cohomological suppliers invoked by the results below assume full
AC, and each item records its exact use. The definitional content below uses no
choice.

**(1) Compact Kähler manifolds.** Let $n\ge1$. A **Kähler manifold** is a complex
manifold $X$ of complex dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]) with complex structure
$J$ and a **Hermitian metric** $g$ — a Riemannian metric
([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) satisfying
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all tangent vectors $v,w$ — whose **real fundamental form**
$\omega(v,w)=g(Jv,w)$ is

- a smooth real 2-form, the section of $\Lambda^2T^*X$ obtained by alternating
  $g(J\cdot,\cdot)$;
- **positive**: $\omega(v,Jv)=g(Jv,Jv)>0$ for every nonzero tangent vector $v$;
- **closed**: $d\omega=0$.

The manifold is **compact Kähler** when the topological space $X$ is compact.

**Orientation.** For a complex basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of a tangent space $T_xX$,
the ordered real basis $(v_1,Jv_1,\dots,v_n,Jv_n)$ is declared **positive**. This
is well defined: two complex bases differ by a complex-linear automorphism, whose
real determinant is the square of the modulus of its complex determinant and so
is positive, and the local orientations therefore glue along holomorphic charts
to a global orientation of $X$. Let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be a $g$-orthonormal complex
frame, so $g(v_j,v_k)=\delta_{jk}$ and $g(v_j,Jv_k)=0$, and let $e_j=g(v_j,\cdot)$ and
$f_j=g(Jv_j,\cdot)$ be the metric-dual covectors. Then
$(e_1,f_1,\dots,e_n,f_n)$ is a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe,
$f_j=-Je_j$ for the pullback action $(J\alpha)(v)=\alpha(Jv)$ of $J$ on
covectors, and

$$\omega=\sum_{j=1}^n e_j\wedge f_j .$$

The **oriented volume form** is the top form

$$dV:=\frac{\omega^n}{n!}=e_1\wedge f_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_n\wedge f_n ,$$

which evaluates to $1$ on each positively oriented $g$-orthonormal frame.

**Complex dimension zero.** For $n=0$ a complex manifold is a discrete space and
compactness makes it a finite set of points with its unique complex structure;
there are no tangent vectors and no forms of positive degree, $\omega=0$, and the
operators $L,\Lambda,\partial,\bar\partial,d,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ and
all Laplacians introduced below are zero. The Hodge star is the identity on
degree zero, and $dV$ is the counting measure.

**(2) Complex-valued forms and Kähler operators.** Let $X$ be compact Kähler.
Write $\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth $k$-forms, the
complex-linear extension of the real forms of
[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]; the Hodge star $*$ of
[[def-riemannian-hodge-star]] extends complex-linearly, and for
$\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ the **integral inner product**

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=\int_X\alpha\wedge*\bar\beta$$

is complex-linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second; the
integral is that of
[[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-top-form-on-an-oriented-manifold]] and
the integrand is $\lvert\alpha\rvert^2\,dV$ when $\beta=\alpha$, so the pairing
is a positive definite Hermitian form. In holomorphic charts

$$\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\Omega^{p,q}(X),\qquad d=\partial+\bar\partial ,$$

with $\partial$ and $\bar\partial$ of bidegree $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$
([[def-bigraded-complex-differential-forms]]); the decomposition is independent
of the holomorphic chart because holomorphic chart changes preserve bidegree.

Put $L=\omega\wedge$, so that $L:\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)\to\Omega^{k+2}(X;\mathbb C)$,
and let $\Lambda,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ be the formal adjoints of
$L,\partial,\bar\partial,d$ with respect to $\langle\,,\rangle$; existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[lem-formal-adjoints-of-differential-operators-exist-and-are-unique]], applied
to the bundle of complex-valued forms with the metric of
[[prop-riemannian-metrics-induce-metrics-on-dual-tensor-and-exterior-bundles]]
and the density $dV$. The **Laplacians** are

$$\Delta_d=dd^*+d^*d,\qquad \Delta_\partial=\partial\partial^*+\partial^*\partial,\qquad \Delta_{\bar\partial}=\bar\partial\bar\partial^*+\bar\partial^*\bar\partial ,$$

and $\epsilon(k)=(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$.

**(3) Rational pure Hodge structures.** Let $k\in\mathbb Z$. A **rational pure
Hodge structure of weight $k$** is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space
$V$ together with a direct-sum decomposition by $\mathbb C$-subspaces

$$V_{\mathbb C}=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}V^{p,q},\qquad \overline{V^{p,q}}=V^{q,p},$$

where conjugation is the $\mathbb C$-antilinear involution
$v\otimes\lambda\mapsto v\otimes\bar\lambda$. The sum is finite because
$V_{\mathbb C}$ is finite dimensional, and it is direct by definition. The **Weil
operator** $C$ is the $\mathbb C$-linear endomorphism of $V_{\mathbb C}$ acting
as $i^{p-q}$ on $V^{p,q}$; the conjugation symmetry makes $C$ commute with
conjugation, so $C$ is the complexification of a real-linear endomorphism
of $V_{\mathbb R}=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$. It need not preserve $V$.

A **polarization** of such a Hodge structure is a nondegenerate $\mathbb Q$-bilinear
form $Q:V\times V\to\mathbb Q$, extended $\mathbb C$-bilinearly to $V_{\mathbb C}$,
such that

- $Q(y,x)=(-1)^kQ(x,y)$ for all $x,y$;
- $Q(V^{p,q},V^{a,b})=0$ unless $(a,b)=(q,p)$;
- $h(x,y)=Q(Cx,\bar y)$ is a positive definite Hermitian form on $V_{\mathbb C}$.

A **rational sub-Hodge structure** is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace
$U\subseteq V$ with $U_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}(U_{\mathbb C}\cap V^{p,q})$.
The **Tate shift** $V(-r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, keeps the underlying $\mathbb Q$-vector
space, the Weil operator and $Q$ as they are and moves the bidegrees to
$(p+r,q+r)$, so that the weight becomes $k+2r$; equivalently, $(V(-r))^{p,q}=V^{p-r,q-r}$.

Let $n\ge0$, let $V$ be a real inner product space of dimension $2n$, and let
$J:V\to V$ be a compatible complex structure ($J^2=-\mathrm{id}$ and
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all $v,w$). Let $\omega\in\bigwedge^2V$ satisfy
$\omega(v,w)=-g(Jv,w)$ for all $v,w$, and orient $V$ so that $\omega^n/n!$ is a
positive volume form. These are the form-side conventions of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]]: $V$ is the
cotangent space at a point, $J$ acts on forms by pullback, and $\omega$ is the
fundamental form. Write $h$ for the induced determinant pairing on the complexified exterior
algebra $\bigwedge^\bullet V_{\mathbb C}$, extended sesquilinearly from $g$
with distinct degrees orthogonal and conjugate-linearity in the second variable, put $L=\omega\wedge$, let $\Lambda=L^*$ be the adjoint
with respect to $h$, and put $H=[L,\Lambda]$ and
$W=\exp L\exp(-\Lambda)\exp L$. Degrees of exterior powers below range over $0\le k\le2n$ (exterior powers
outside this range are zero). Let $J$ also denote the algebra endomorphism
$J(x\wedge y)=Jx\wedge Jy$ of $\bigwedge^\bullet V_{\mathbb C}$, let
$\bigwedge^{p,q}V_{\mathbb C}$ be the span of $p$-fold wedges of
$V^{1,0}=\ker(J-i)$ with $q$-fold wedges of $V^{0,1}=\ker(J+i)$, and let $*$ be
the complex-linear extension of the Hodge star of $V$ and
$\epsilon(k)=(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$.

Then the following hold.

1. $H=[L,\Lambda]$ satisfies $[L,\Lambda]=H$, $H=(k-n)\mathrm{id}$ on
   $\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$, $[H,L]=2L$ and $[H,\Lambda]=-2\Lambda$.
2. Every $\alpha\in\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$ has a unique decomposition
   $\alpha=\sum_{r\ge\max(0,k-n)}L^ru_r$ with $\Lambda u_r=0$ and
   $u_r\in\bigwedge^{k-2r}V_{\mathbb C}$; all but finitely many terms vanish,
   and the projections $\alpha\mapsto u_r$ are rational polynomials in
   $L,\Lambda$ on each fixed degree.
3. If $0\le t\le n$ and $u\in\bigwedge^tV_{\mathbb C}$ is primitive
   ($\Lambda u=0$) of degree $t$,
   then $L^{n-t+1}u=0$ and
   $$\Lambda^sL^ru=\frac{r!}{(r-s)!}\frac{(n-t-r+s)!}{(n-t-r)!}L^{r-s}u\qquad(0\le s\le r\le n-t);$$
   no nonzero primitive element has degree $t>n$; for $k\le n$ an element of
   $\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$ is primitive exactly when $L^{n-k+1}u=0$; and
   $L^{n-k}:\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}\to\bigwedge^{2n-k}V_{\mathbb C}$ is an
   isomorphism for $k\le n$.
4. $J=i^{p-q}$ on $\bigwedge^{p,q}V_{\mathbb C}$, and
   $W\alpha=\epsilon(k)J*\alpha$ for every $\alpha$ of degree $k$. If $0\le k=p+q\le n$ and $u$ is
   primitive of type $(p,q)$, then
   $$*u=\frac{\epsilon(k)i^{q-p}}{(n-k)!}L^{n-k}u .$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
analytic suppliers below. Let $X$ be a compact Kähler $n$-fold with Kähler form
$\omega$, in the conventions of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]], and put
$L=[\omega]\smile(-)$ on cohomology. Then the following hold.

- $L^{n-k}:H^k(X;\mathbb R)\to H^{2n-k}(X;\mathbb R)$ is an isomorphism for
  $0\le k\le n$.
- Harmonic representatives transport $(L,\Lambda,H)$ to an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$
  action: $L$ is cup product with $[\omega]$, $\Lambda$ on cohomology means
  applying $\Lambda$ to the harmonic representative and not to an arbitrary
  closed form, $H$ acts by $\deg-n$, and
  $[L,\Lambda]=H$, $[H,L]=2L$, $[H,\Lambda]=-2\Lambda$ hold on cohomology.
- Primitive cohomology is
  $P^k=\{a\in H^k(X;\mathbb R):\text{the harmonic representative of }a\text{ lies in }\ker\Lambda\}$,
  and for $0\le k\le n$ one has
  $P^k=\ker\bigl(L^{n-k+1}:H^k(X;\mathbb R)\to H^{2n-k+2}(X;\mathbb R)\bigr)$;
  for every $k$,
  $$H^k(X;\mathbb R)=\bigoplus_{r\ge\max(0,k-n)}L^rP^{k-2r},$$
  and a class of type $(p,q)$ has primitive components of type $(p-r,q-r)$.
- If $[\omega]$ is the real image of a rational class
  $\ell\in H^2(X;\mathbb Q)$, all these decompositions and $L$-isomorphisms are
  rational, and they remain isomorphisms after extension to every
  characteristic-zero field.

Assume AC. For a compact Kähler manifold $X$ in the sense of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]], every de
Rham class has a unique smooth harmonic representative and
$$H^k(X;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^{p,q}(X),\qquad \overline{H^{p,q}(X)}=H^{q,p}(X).$$
Here $H^{p,q}(X)$ is precisely the set of classes with a $d$-closed smooth
representative of type $(p,q)$, so the decomposition is independent of the
Kähler metric. Writing $\Omega_X^p$ for the sheaf of holomorphic $p$-forms (the
kernel of $\bar\partial$ on the sheaf $\mathcal A^{p,0}$ of smooth $(p,0)$-forms),
$H^{p,q}(X)$ is isomorphic to $H^q(X,\Omega_X^p)$, the sheaf cohomology of
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]. The Hodge filtration
$F^a=\bigoplus_{p\ge a}H^{p,k-p}$ of $H^k(X;\mathbb C)$ equals the filtration
induced by the holomorphic-degree filtration of the de Rham complex, whose
spectral sequence has $E_1^{p,q}=H^q(X,\Omega_X^p)$ and degenerates at $E_1$.
Pullback by holomorphic maps of compact Kähler manifolds and cup product
preserve Hodge type, so $H^k(X;\mathbb Q)$ is a functorial rational pure Hodge
structure.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth boundaryless
$m$-manifold and let $\alpha\in\Omega^m(M)$ be a smooth real or complex top form.
Let $J_M:H^m_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\to H^m_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R)$ be the de Rham
comparison of [[thm-de-rham-theorem]] for real forms, extended
complex-linearly with codomain $H^m_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb C)$ for complex
forms. Use the smooth-orientation normalization: a positively oriented affine
$m$-simplex represents the positive local homology generator at each interior
point. Let $[M]\in H_m(M;\mathbb R)$ be the real fundamental class of
[[def-fundamental-class-of-a-compact-oriented-manifold]], and let
$\langle\,,\rangle$ be the Kronecker evaluation pairing
([[def-kronecker-evaluation-pairing]]). Then

$$\langle J_M[\alpha],[M]\rangle=\int_M\alpha .$$

Consequently, if $c_1,\dots,c_r\in H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)$ with
$\sum_i\deg c_i=m$ are represented by closed smooth forms $\alpha_i$, then

$$\langle J_M(c_1)\smile\cdots\smile J_M(c_r),[M]\rangle=\int_M\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_r .$$

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold with boundary, $n\geq1$, and let $\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(M)$. With $j:\partial M\hookrightarrow M$ and the outward-normal-first orientation,
$$\int_M d\eta=\int_{\partial M}j^*\eta.$$
An empty boundary contributes zero; in dimension one its integral is a finite signed sum of point values.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional Hausdorff
second-countable smooth manifold, possibly with boundary or empty, and let
$L\to M$ be a smooth complex line bundle with a supplied Hermitian metric and
Hermitian connection $\nabla$. Write $\Omega_\nabla$ for its curvature and
$c_1(L):=e(L_{\mathbb R})$ for the published integral line class, using the
complex orientation on the underlying real plane. Let
$$\rho_M:H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H^2(M;\mathbb R)$$
be induced by $\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$. Under the natural de Rham
isomorphism $J_M$,
$$J_M\left[ -\frac{\Omega_\nabla}{2\pi i}\right]=\rho_M(c_1(L)).$$
For a disconnected base the same line-class convention is understood on each
component; the global class is the Euler class displayed above.

If $\nabla'$ is any complex connection on $L$, not necessarily metric
compatible, then
$$\left[-\frac{\Omega_{\nabla'}}{2\pi i}\right]=\iota_M\!\left(J_M^{-1}\rho_M(c_1(L))\right)\quad\text{in }H^2_{\rm dR}(M;\mathbb C),$$
where $\iota_M$ is induced by including real-valued forms into complex-valued
forms. Thus the arbitrary-connection class is identified with the same real
class by the degree-one transgression.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
Jacobian-criterion, ample-powers, Chern-form and comparison suppliers below.
Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex scheme of pure dimension $n\ge0$.

Then the closed points of $X$ carry a structure of **complex manifold**
$X^{\mathrm{an}}$, its **analytification**: if $X\ne\varnothing$ and $n\ge1$
this is a compact Hausdorff second-countable smooth complex manifold of complex
dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]); if $n=0$ it is the
finite discrete set $X(\mathbb C)$ with its unique complex structure in the
convention of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]]; and if
$X=\varnothing$ then $X^{\mathrm{an}}=\varnothing$. Every standard smooth
algebraic chart of $X$ becomes a holomorphic chart of $X^{\mathrm{an}}$, and
more generally, every morphism between smooth separated finite-type complex schemes of pure dimensions induces a holomorphic map between their analytifications. These analytifications are constructed by the same charts and need not be compact; separatedness and finite type ensure that they are Hausdorff and second-countable.

Moreover, for every ample invertible sheaf $A$ on $X$ there is a smooth
positive closed real $(1,1)$-form $\eta_A$ on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$ whose de Rham
class is the real image of the topological first Chern class
$c_1(A):=c_1(A^{\mathrm{an}})\in H^2(X^{\mathrm{an}};\mathbb Z)$:
$$J_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}[\eta_A]=\rho_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}\bigl(c_1(A)\bigr),$$
where $J$ is the de Rham comparison and $\rho$ the change of coefficients
$\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$
([[lem-rational-cohomology-scalar-comparison-for-compact-smooth-manifolds]]).
In dimension $n=0$ and for $X=\varnothing$ every $2$-form and every degree-two
cohomology class is zero and $\eta_A=0$, so the identity holds trivially.

Assume AC. For a compact smooth manifold $X$, the natural coefficient maps
induce isomorphisms $H^k(X;\mathbb Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}F\cong H^k(X;F)$ for
every characteristic-zero field $F$, finite-dimensional in each degree. For
$F=\mathbb R,\mathbb C$ these identify singular cohomology with the real or
complex de Rham cohomology. They preserve cup products and are natural for maps
between such manifolds. No ordered-field or positivity structure is asserted
for a general $F$.

The derived augmentation is computed by a normalized double complex; before normalization its spectral sequence has first page $R^j q_{p*}F_p$ and alternating face differential. A common internal lower bound makes every total-degree diagonal finite. The same construction works for strict bisimplicial diagrams and is compatible with composition of derived right adjoints to exact inverse image. If $Z_\bullet$ is the Čech nerve of a map $P\to S$ admitting local sections, inverse image gives an equivalence from $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(S))$ to the full derived subcategory with Cartesian cohomology. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty:

and derived-incidence suppliers of the Verdier theorem. For analytic algebraic maps on its proved constructible subcategory, the six operations $f^*,Rf_*,Rf_!,f^!,\otimes_k^L,R\mathcal Hom$ have their three adjunctions, composition and identity comparisons, ordinary proper and extraordinary proper base change, projection formula, support localization, dualizing transitivity and trace. The comparisons commute with Cartesian pasting, composition of maps, evaluation and trace, giving a coherent pull-push product calculus. For a locally trivial product projection with finite-type smooth fibre

the ordinary analytic sheaf operations restrict to bounded algebraically constructible complexes $D_c^b(-;k)$ ([[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]]): $f^*\dashv Rf_*$, $Rf_!\dashv f^!$, the tensor/internal-Hom adjunction, coherent composition, support localization, ordinary and extraordinary proper base change, the projection formula and trace. Proper $f$ satisfies $Rf_!=Rf_*$. Verdier duality is involutive there and exchanges these adjoints. On a smooth complex $d$-fold $\omega_X=k_X[2d]$, and for a smooth map of relative dimension $d$, $f^!=f^*[2d]$.

derivations.claim: Bounded strict model and finite diagonals. Choose a cochain lower bound $a$ with $F$ represented by a strict complex vanishing in degrees $q<a$, possible because $F$ is cohomologically bounded; by [F1] exact inverse image preserves vanishing there, so the same $a$ bounds every $F_p$, and right-derived pushforward produces a functorial double model in degrees $p\geq0$, $q\geq a$. In total degree $m$ only $0\leq p\leq m-a$ occurs, so every diagonal is finite and [F2]'s strict total model may be used with either totalization. Take the cone of the augmented map $F\to\operatorname{Tot}_pRf_{p*}F_p$, place the augmentation in column $p=-1$, and filter by $p$; each total degree of the cone involves only finitely many columns. At a point $x\in X$ the stalk of the cone is the cone of the stalk map, and because the stalk functor is exact and commutes with the finite column sums, this stalk carries the induced finite filtration, whose first page in internal degree $q$ is the augmented horizontal row of $H^q$ of the stalk complexes. [F1, F2, given]

The stalk row and one chosen point. Fix $x\in X$ and put $K=F_x$, a complex of $k$-vector spaces with $H^q(K)=H^q(F)_x$; surjectivity of $f$ makes the fiber $S=Y_x$ nonempty. By the proper base change and fiber-pullback clauses of [F1], the stalk at $x$ of $Rf_{p*}F_p$ is $R\Gamma(S^{p+1},K)$ with $K$ the constant derived pullback, and these identifications are natural for all face and degeneracy maps, so the first page of the stalk row in internal degree $q$ is
$$H^q(K)\xrightarrow{\delta_{-1}}H^q(S,K)\xrightarrow{\delta_0}H^q(S^2,K)\xrightarrow{\delta_1}\cdots,$$
where $\delta_p$ is the alternating sum of the pullbacks along the $(p+2)$ coordinate-deletion maps $d_i:S^{p+2}\to S^{p+1}$. Choose one point $y\in S$; no assertion that any positive cohomology group of $S$ vanishes, or that $S$ is connected or smooth, is made or used. [F1, A1, step 1.1]

Explicit contraction of every augmented row. For $r\geq0$ let $\mathrm{ins}_r:S^r\to S^{r+1}$ insert $y$ as first coordinate, with $S^0=\mathrm{pt}$; so $\mathrm{ins}_0$ is the point $y$ itself. The deletion and insertion maps satisfy $d_0\,\mathrm{ins}_{r+1}=\mathrm{id}$ and $d_i\,\mathrm{ins}_{r+1}=\mathrm{ins}_r\,d_{i-1}$ for $i>0$. Put $h_{p+1}:=\mathrm{ins}_{p+1}^*:H^q(S^{p+2},K)\to H^q(S^{p+1},K)$ and $h_0:=\mathrm{ins}_0^*:H^q(S,K)\to H^q(K)$, with $\delta_{-1}$ the constant pullback of the projection $S\to\mathrm{pt}$. Applying the two identities termwise gives $h_{p+1}\delta_p+\delta_{p-1}h_p=\mathrm{id}$ for every $p\geq0$: the $i=0$ term of $h_{p+1}\delta_p$ is the identity, and the terms $i>0$ are the negatives of $\delta_{p-1}h_p$; moreover $h_0\delta_{-1}=\mathrm{id}$, because the projection followed by the chosen point is the identity of $\mathrm{pt}$. Hence every augmented horizontal row is contractible, in particular exact, in every internal degree $q$, using only functorial pullback on cohomology. [step 1.2, algebra]

Conclusion and naturality. By step 2.1 the next page of the spectral sequence of the stalk cone vanishes at every stalk, and by step 1.1 its filtration is finite in each total degree, so [F3] identifies the associated graded of the stalk cohomology with zero in every degree; the stalk of the cone at $x$ is therefore acyclic, for every $x\in X$. A complex of sheaves whose stalks are all acyclic has zero cohomology sheaves, hence is acyclic; this proves the asserted quasi-isomorphism $F\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}Rf_{p*}F_p$. All algebraic base changes of $f$ remain proper surjective, and the identifications of steps 1.2-3.1 are pullbacks of one another by the Cartesian-pasting naturality of [F1], so the pulled-back assertion follows without choosing compatible points; coefficient morphisms act componentwise by the same naturality. For the global statement use [F2]’s simplicial injective model: its levelwise injectives push forward to injectives, since inverse image is exact and left adjoint to direct image. The total is a bounded-below complex of injectives, because each total degree is a finite sum. Thus global sections compute its derived global sections termwise; derived composition in [F1] identifies the columns with $R\Gamma(Y_p,F_p)$, giving $R\Gamma(X,F)\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_pR\Gamma(Y_p,F_p)$. The Axiom of Choice is inherited exactly through [A1]. [F1, F3, A1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty:

The comparisons commute with Cartesian pasting, composition of maps, evaluation and trace, giving a coherent pull-push product calculus. derivations.claim: Bounded strict model and finite diagonals. Choose a cochain lower bound $a$ with $F$ represented by a strict complex vanishing in degrees $q<a$, possible because $F$ is cohomologically bounded; by [F1] exact inverse image preserves vanishing there, so the same $a$ bounds every $F_p$, and right-derived pushforward produces a functorial double model in degrees $p\geq0$, $q\geq a$. In total degree $m$ only $0\leq p\leq m-a$ occurs, so every diagonal is finite and [F2]'s strict total model may be used with either totalization. Take the cone of the augmented map $F\to\operatorname{Tot}_pRf_{p*}F_p$, place the augmentation in column $p=-1$, and filter by $p$; each total degree of the cone involves only finitely many columns. At a point $x\in X$ the stalk of the cone is the cone of the stalk map, and because the stalk functor is exact and commutes with the finite column sums, this stalk carries the induced finite filtration, whose first page in internal degree $q$ is the augmented horizontal row of $H^q$ of the stalk complexes. [F1, F2, given]

The stalk row and one chosen point. Fix $x\in X$ and put $K=F_x$, a complex of $k$-vector spaces with $H^q(K)=H^q(F)_x$; surjectivity of $f$ makes the fiber $S=Y_x$ nonempty. By the proper base change and fiber-pullback clauses of [F1], the stalk at $x$ of $Rf_{p*}F_p$ is $R\Gamma(S^{p+1},K)$ with $K$ the constant derived pullback, and these identifications are natural for all face and degeneracy maps, so the first page of the stalk row in internal degree $q$ is
$$H^q(K)\xrightarrow{\delta_{-1}}H^q(S,K)\xrightarrow{\delta_0}H^q(S^2,K)\xrightarrow{\delta_1}\cdots,$$
where $\delta_p$ is the alternating sum of the pullbacks along the $(p+2)$ coordinate-deletion maps $d_i:S^{p+2}\to S^{p+1}$. Choose one point $y\in S$; no assertion that any positive cohomology group of $S$ vanishes, or that $S$ is connected or smooth, is made or used. [F1, A1, step 1.1]

Explicit contraction of every augmented row. For $r\geq0$ let $\mathrm{ins}_r:S^r\to S^{r+1}$ insert $y$ as first coordinate, with $S^0=\mathrm{pt}$; so $\mathrm{ins}_0$ is the point $y$ itself. The deletion and insertion maps satisfy $d_0\,\mathrm{ins}_{r+1}=\mathrm{id}$ and $d_i\,\mathrm{ins}_{r+1}=\mathrm{ins}_r\,d_{i-1}$ for $i>0$. Put $h_{p+1}:=\mathrm{ins}_{p+1}^*:H^q(S^{p+2},K)\to H^q(S^{p+1},K)$ and $h_0:=\mathrm{ins}_0^*:H^q(S,K)\to H^q(K)$, with $\delta_{-1}$ the constant pullback of the projection $S\to\mathrm{pt}$. Applying the two identities termwise gives $h_{p+1}\delta_p+\delta_{p-1}h_p=\mathrm{id}$ for every $p\geq0$: the $i=0$ term of $h_{p+1}\delta_p$ is the identity, and the terms $i>0$ are the negatives of $\delta_{p-1}h_p$; moreover $h_0\delta_{-1}=\mathrm{id}$, because the projection followed by the chosen point is the identity of $\mathrm{pt}$. Hence every augmented horizontal row is contractible, in particular exact, in every internal degree $q$, using only functorial pullback on cohomology. [step 1.2, algebra]

Conclusion and naturality. By step 2.1 the next page of the spectral sequence of the stalk cone vanishes at every stalk, and by step 1.1 its filtration is finite in each total degree, so [F3] identifies the associated graded of the stalk cohomology with zero in every degree; the stalk of the cone at $x$ is therefore acyclic, for every $x\in X$. A complex of sheaves whose stalks are all acyclic has zero cohomology sheaves, hence is acyclic; this proves the asserted quasi-isomorphism $F\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}Rf_{p*}F_p$. All algebraic base changes of $f$ remain proper surjective, and the identifications of steps 1.2-3.1 are pullbacks of one another by the Cartesian-pasting naturality of [F1], so the pulled-back assertion follows without choosing compatible points; coefficient morphisms act componentwise by the same naturality. For the global statement use [F2]’s simplicial injective model: its levelwise injectives push forward to injectives, since inverse image is exact and left adjoint to direct image. The total is a bounded-below complex of injectives, because each total degree is a finite sum. Thus global sections compute its derived global sections termwise; derived composition in [F1] identifies the columns with $R\Gamma(Y_p,F_p)$, giving $R\Gamma(X,F)\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_pR\Gamma(Y_p,F_p)$. The Axiom of Choice is inherited exactly through [A1]. [F1, F3, A1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the supplied injective-resolution six-functor construction. Let $f:Y\to X$ be a proper surjective morphism of finite-type complex algebraic varieties, and let $F\in D^b_c(X;k)$ for a field $k$. Write $Y_p=Y\times_X\cdots\times_XY$ with $p+1$ factors, $f_p:Y_p\to X$, and $F_p=f_p^*F$. In the analytic topology of [[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]] the natural augmented derived Cech map is a quasi-isomorphism:
$$F\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}Rf_{p*}F_p.$$
Here totalization is the normalized or unnormalized alternating-face total supplied by the simplicial-derived construction. There is one fixed lower cochain bound; consequently its diagonals are finite in every degree. The claim commutes with arbitrary algebraic base change and coefficient morphisms. In particular $R\Gamma(X,F)\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_pR\Gamma(Y_p,F_p)$. Individual fibers of $f$ need not be cohomologically acyclic, connected, or smooth.

Fix an algebraically closed field $k$. The affine models used here are polynomial zero sets $Z\subseteq k^n$, including empty and reducible sets. Their closed subsets are common zero loci of polynomial families, relative to $Z$. Intersections combine equations, and finite unions use products of equations, so these are the closed sets of a topology.

For an open $U\subseteq Z$, let $\mathcal O_Z(U)$ consist of functions $U\to k$ locally equal to $a/b$ for polynomials $a,b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the chosen neighbourhood. Pointwise operations and restriction make these sets a sheaf of $k$-algebras: quotient expressions persist on restriction, and functions that agree locally glue uniquely with the same local quotient property. At a point z its stalk is the ring of germs of such functions. Evaluation at z maps it onto k, with kernel the germs vanishing at z. A germ nonzero at z is invertible: shrink to where its numerator and denominator are both nonzero and interchange them. Thus the kernel is the unique maximal ideal. These affine models are locally ringed spaces in the sense of [[def-locally-ringed-space]], with residue fields canonically k.

A **classical algebraic prevariety** over k is a quasi-compact locally ringed space with a structure sheaf of k-algebras, covered by open subspaces isomorphic over k to these affine models. Here quasi-compact means every open cover has a finite subcover. Equivalently it admits a finite affine-model cover. To justify the converse, each affine model is quasi-compact: polynomial principal opens $D_Z(h)=\{z:h(z)\ne0\}$ form a basis. Given an open cover, take all h whose principal opens lie in a member. Their principal opens cover Z. The ideal generated by these h in $k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$ is finitely generated by [[thm-hilbert-basis-theorem]], iterated from the field k. Express finitely many generators using finitely many of the original h. Those finitely many h have the same common zero locus as the whole ideal, hence their principal opens still cover Z and yield a finite subcover. The empty model has the empty subcover. A finite union of quasi-compact subspaces is quasi-compact.

A map is **regular** when it is a morphism of locally ringed spaces as in [[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]] whose sheaf maps respect k. For these function sheaves its sheaf map is necessarily pullback of functions: the local stalk map induces a k-map between residue fields k, hence the identity, so the value of a pulled-back section at x is its value at the image of x. Conversely, continuous pullback of local regular functions gives a local stalk map because a function vanishing at the image vanishes after pullback.

Regularity can therefore be checked on affine charts: near every source point choose a target affine chart containing its image and an open neighbourhood in a source affine chart mapped into it; the target coordinate functions must pull back to locally polynomial quotients. This condition also implies continuity. Indeed zero sets of locally polynomial quotients are locally polynomial zero sets, hence closed; pulling back polynomial equations consequently gives closed sets. Substitution then pulls every local quotient on the target back to a local quotient on the source, using this continuity to restrict to its domain and its nonvanishing denominator. Thus the chart condition and the locally ringed-space definition agree.

A prevariety is **separated** when the equalizer of every pair of regular maps into it, from any classical prevariety, is closed. A **classical algebraic variety** is a separated prevariety. Here varieties may be reducible or empty; an **irreducible classical variety** is nonempty and irreducible in the sense of [[def-irreducible-topological-space-and-subset]]. These definitions and the local verifications above use no Axiom of Choice.

Let $X$ be a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]: a separated
quasi-compact locally ringed space over $\mathbb C$ with a finite cover by
affine models $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the morphisms being the regular maps,
i.e. the morphisms of locally ringed spaces over $\mathbb C$
([[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]]).

(a) **Analytic topology.** An affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ carries the
subspace topology of the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb C^n$
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]],
[[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). If $Z_1,Z_2\subseteq X$ are affine
models and $\varphi:Z_1\to Z_2$ is the structure-sheaf isomorphism, then on
$Z_1\cap Z_2$ the maps $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are given locally by
polynomial quotient functions
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]) and are
therefore continuous for the Euclidean topologies: polynomial functions are
continuous, and a quotient is continuous wherever its denominator does not
vanish ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]],
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). Hence the topologies transported
from the two affine models agree on the overlap, so the affine-model topologies
glue to a unique topology on the underlying set of $X$
([[def-topological-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]): the **analytic
topology** of $X$. Every regular map of complex classical varieties is
continuous for the analytic topologies, by the same local description
([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and the analytic topology refines the Zariski
topology because polynomial zero sets are Euclidean closed. Whenever a complex
algebraic variety is used as a topological space below it carries the analytic
topology, and each subvariety carries the subspace topology.

(b) **Smooth points.** Let $S$ be a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ and let
$x\in S$. The point $x$ is a **smooth point of $S$** if its algebraic local ring
$\mathcal O_{S,x}$ is a regular local ring: a nonzero Noetherian local ring
whose maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_x$ satisfies
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2)=\dim\mathcal O_{S,x}$
([[def-embedding-dimension-and-regular-local-ring]]). The residue field at a
classical complex point is $\mathbb C$. The variety $S$ is **smooth** if every
point is smooth. This intrinsic algebraic condition does not require a Zariski
neighbourhood to be algebraically isomorphic to an open subset of affine space.

(c) **Finite smooth algebraic stratifications.** A **finite smooth algebraic
stratification with the frontier condition** of $X$ is a finite decomposition
$X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty connected
locally closed subsets $S_\alpha\subseteq X$ — the **strata** — such that each
$S_\alpha$, with its reduced induced algebraic structure, is a smooth algebraic
subvariety of $X$; and such that for every $\alpha$ the closure
$\overline{S_\alpha}$ of $S_\alpha$ in $X$ is a union of strata. The latter is
the **frontier condition**: the frontier
$\overline{S_\alpha}\setminus S_\alpha$ of every stratum is a union of strata
([[def-connected-space]], [[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]).

**The induced structure is the polynomial-quotient function sheaf, not a
restriction of $\mathcal O_X$.** A locally closed $S\subseteq X$ is, locally
inside an affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the set of points with $h\neq0$
and $f_1=\dots=f_r=0$ for polynomials $h,f_1,\dots,f_r$ on $Z$
([[def-constructible-subset-variety]],
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]); the map
$z\mapsto(z,1/h(z))$ identifies it with the affine model
$\{(z,t):th(z)=1,\ f_1(z)=\dots=f_r(z)=0\}\subseteq\mathbb C^{n+1}$, and its
**reduced induced structure sheaf** is the one transported along this
identification: locally functions of the form $a/b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the
set. The ambient restriction $\mathcal O_X|_S$ is not used, since already at the
origin of the affine line the ambient stalk is the local ring of the line while
the stalk of the reduced point is $\mathbb C$. An open subset of an affine model
is a union of principal open subsets, and each principal open subset is again an
affine model, so every locally closed subvariety of $X$ is a classical variety
for the induced structure sheaf. No existence theorem for stratifications, no
common-refinement theorem and no choice principle is asserted: nothing is
selected, and all cited suppliers are choice-free.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

**A point outside $X$, named rather than assumed.** Put

$$\infty \;:=\; \{\, y \in X : y \notin y \,\},$$

a set by Separation. Then $\infty \notin X$: were $\infty \in X$, the defining
condition applied to $\infty$ itself would give
$\infty \in \infty \iff \infty \notin \infty$. So no hypothesis about $X$ is
needed to obtain a point outside it, and the construction below is available for
every space.

**The space.** Put $X^{*} := X \cup \{\infty\}$ and

$$\mathcal{T}^{*} \;:=\; \mathcal{T} \;\cup\; \{\, X^{*} \setminus C \;:\; C \subseteq X,\ C \text{ closed in } X \text{ and a compact subset of } X \,\} .$$

The pair $(X^{*}, \mathcal{T}^{*})$ is the **one-point compactification**, or
**Alexandroff compactification**, of $X$. Members of $\mathcal{T}$ are said to be
of the **first kind** and the sets $X^{*} \setminus C$ of the **second kind**; a
set of the second kind is exactly an open set of $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ containing
$\infty$, since a member of $\mathcal{T}$ is a subset of $X$, and the set $C$ is
recovered from it as $C = X^{*} \setminus (X^{*} \setminus C)$.

**$\mathcal{T}^{*}$ is a topology on $X^{*}$, and this is discharged here.**
Throughout, "closed" and "compact" without qualification mean closed in $X$ and a
compact subset of $X$ ([[def-compact-space]]); two facts about such sets are used
and both are [[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]: a subset of a
compact $C$ that is closed in $X$ is closed in the subspace $C$
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]) and hence compact, and a union of two compact
subsets is compact.

*(T1).* $\varnothing \in \mathcal{T}$, and $X^{*} = X^{*} \setminus \varnothing$
is of the second kind, $\varnothing$ being closed in $X$ and compact.

*(T2).* Let $\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{T}^{*}$, let $\mathcal{S}_1$ be the
members of $\mathcal{S}$ lying in $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{S}_2$ the rest, so
that every member of $\mathcal{S}_2$ is of the second kind. If
$\mathcal{S}_2 = \varnothing$ then $\bigcup \mathcal{S} = \bigcup \mathcal{S}_1$
lies in $\mathcal{T}$ by (T2) in $X$. Otherwise put
$U := \bigcup \mathcal{S}_1 \in \mathcal{T}$ and
$\mathcal{D} := \{\, X^{*} \setminus O : O \in \mathcal{S}_2 \,\}$, a nonempty
family of closed compact subsets of $X$, and $C_0 := \bigcap \mathcal{D}$. Then
$C_0$ is closed by (C2) of [[def-topological-space]], and it is a closed subset of
any one member of $\mathcal{D}$, hence compact. Now

$$\bigcup \mathcal{S} \;=\; U \cup (X^{*} \setminus C_0) \;=\; X^{*} \setminus (C_0 \setminus U),$$

and $C_0 \setminus U = C_0 \cap (X \setminus U)$ is closed in $X$ and a subset of
the compact $C_0$, hence compact; so $\bigcup \mathcal{S}$ is of the second kind.

*(T3).* For $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ the intersection lies in $\mathcal{T}$ by (T3)
in $X$. For two sets of the second kind,
$(X^{*} \setminus C) \cap (X^{*} \setminus D) = X^{*} \setminus (C \cup D)$, and
$C \cup D$ is closed in $X$ and compact as a union of two compact subsets. For one
of each, $\infty \notin U$ gives
$U \cap (X^{*} \setminus C) = U \cap (X \setminus C)$, an intersection of two
members of $\mathcal{T}$.

**Why the compact sets are also required to be closed.** The complement of a
compact set that is not closed in $X$ would not make $\infty$'s neighbourhoods
behave: the union computation in (T2) uses that an intersection of the discarded
sets is again closed, and the intersection of arbitrary compact subsets of a
non-Hausdorff space need not be compact. When $X$ is Hausdorff every compact
subset is closed ([[thm-compact-subset-of-a-hausdorff-space-is-closed]]) and the
two descriptions agree, which is why many texts state the definition without the
word "closed" and silently assume the Hausdorff case.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$(X^{*}, \mathcal{T}^{*})$ be its one-point compactification, with added point
$\infty$ ([[def-one-point-compactification]]). Then:

1. **$X^{*}$ is compact** ([[def-compact-space]]).
2. **$X$ is an open subspace of $X^{*}$**: $X \in \mathcal{T}^{*}$, and the
   subspace topology that $X$ inherits from $X^{*}$
   ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]) is $\mathcal{T}$ itself.
3. **$X$ is dense in $X^{*}$** ([[def-dense-top]]) **if and only if $X$ is not
   compact.**
4. **$X^{*}$ is Hausdorff** ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) **if and only if $X$ is
   locally compact** ([[def-locally-compact-space]]) **and Hausdorff.**

In particular, a locally compact Hausdorff space is an open subspace of a compact
Hausdorff space, which is the reason the construction is made. **No choice
principle is used**: the only cover thinned below is thinned by the indexed form
of [[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], which returns its own indices.

Let
$$S^2:=\{(x,y,t)\in\mathbb R^3:x^2+y^2+t^2=1\}.$$
Define
$$\Sigma(z)=\left(\frac{2\operatorname{Re}z}{1+|z|^2},\ \frac{2\operatorname{Im}z}{1+|z|^2},\ \frac{|z|^2-1}{1+|z|^2}\right)\qquad(z\in\mathbb C)$$
and $\Sigma(\infty)=(0,0,1)$. Then $\Sigma:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to S^2$ is a
homeomorphism, with inverse
$$\Pi(x,y,t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x+iy}{1-t},&(x,y,t)\neq(0,0,1),\\ \infty,&(x,y,t)=(0,0,1).\end{cases}$$

If $f:X\to Y$ is a homotopy equivalence, then for every $n\geq 0$ and every
abelian group $G$ the induced map
$$H_n(f_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(Y;G)$$
is an isomorphism.

For $n\ge1$, $\widetilde H_k(S^n;G)$ is $G$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
For $S^0$, $\widetilde H_0(S^0;G)\cong G$ and all other reduced groups vanish.
Thus $H_0(S^n;G)\cong G$ for $n\ge1$, whereas
$H_0(S^0;G)\cong G\oplus G$.

Assume AC. For every field $k$, every space $X$, and $n\ge0$, evaluation gives a natural $k$-linear isomorphism
$$H^n(X;k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_k(H_n(X;k),k).$$
There is no finite-dimensional hypothesis. The right side is the full algebraic dual.

A morphism $f:X\to Y$ of classical varieties is projective here if there is an integer $N\ge0$ and a factorization $X\hookrightarrow Y\times\mathbf P_k^N\to Y$ in which the first map is a closed immersion and the second is projection. The product and its standard charts are supplied by [[lem-relative-projective-homogeneous-equations]]. A closed immersion in this classical setting is an isomorphism onto a reduced closed subvariety. Morphisms have the general locally ringed-space meaning of [[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]], checked on affine charts.

Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

Assume AC. Let $f:X\to Y$ be one morphism of reduced quasi-projective complex
algebraic varieties, and prescribe finitely many closed or locally closed
algebraic subsets in source and target. There exist finite smooth complex
algebraic Whitney (a),(b) stratifications with frontier on $X$ and $Y$
respecting all prescribed subsets, such that each source stratum maps
surjectively and smoothly onto one target stratum. A further finite algebraic
stratification may be prescribed and refined. The analytic strata are smooth
complex manifolds and the restrictions are smooth submersions. If $f$ is proper
in the analytic topology, in particular if it is a projective algebraic
morphism, the whole restriction $f^{-1}(T)\to T$ over any target stratum is
proper; no restriction of $f$ to a nonclosed individual source stratum is
asserted proper.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) having a neighbourhood basis of contractible open sets at
every point, and let $k$ be a field. Write $k_X$ for its constant sheaf. There
are natural isomorphisms
$$H^q(X,k_X)\cong H^q_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$$
in every degree, where the left side is derived cohomology in the category of
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces (computed with the functorial $k$-linear injective
resolutions supplied by
[[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]; compare
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). The same assertion holds on
every open subset of $X$. In particular a nonempty contractible space with this
local property has constant-sheaf cohomology $k$ in degree zero and zero
otherwise. This applies to every finite-polyhedral open star and to its
nonempty intersection with a closed simplex.

derivations.claim: The space and its two charts. Glue the affine $z$-line and affine $w$-line along $zw=1$. Their regular transition gives a prevariety with a finite affine cover ([F2], [F3]). Its diagonal is closed: on the two same-chart products equality is $z=z'$ or $w=w'$, and on either cross-chart product it is $zw'=1$ or $wz'=1$. Equalizers of regular maps are inverse images of this diagonal, so $S$ is separated. The formulas of [F5] define a homeomorphism from this glued space to $S^2$: in the $w$-chart they become $(2\operatorname{Re}w,-2\operatorname{Im}w,1-|w|^2)/(1+|w|^2)$, including the north pole at $w=0$; the inverse coordinate there is $w=(x-iy)/(1+t)$, continuous near the north pole. In the other chart the formulas and inverse are those of [F5]. Composing with [F5]'s inverse identifies the analytic topology with the one-point compactification of [F4]. In particular $S$ is compact. [F2, F3, F4, F5, construct, algebra]

The map is proper surjective. The unique morphism $f:S\to\mathrm{pt}$ is surjective because $S$ is nonempty. It is projective in the sense of [F9]: the identity is a closed immersion $S\hookrightarrow\mathrm{pt}\times\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)$ onto a reduced closed subvariety, and the projection to the point is the structure map. By the properness clause of [F10], a projective algebraic morphism is proper in the analytic topology; hence $f$ is a proper surjective morphism of finite-type complex algebraic varieties, and [F1] applies to it. The single fiber is not acyclic. The field-dual corollary [F8] then gives $H^2(S;k)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_k(H_2(S;k),k)\cong k\neq0$, since $k$ is a field. The sphere is metric with a contractible-open neighbourhood basis, and these properties transfer through the homeomorphism, so [F11] identifies this singular cohomology group with the actual derived constant-sheaf group $H^2(S,k_S)$.
