Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the supplied injective-resolution six-functor construction. Let $f:Y\to X$ be a proper surjective morphism of finite-type complex algebraic varieties, and let $F\in D^b_c(X;k)$ for a field $k$. Write $Y_p=Y\times_X\cdots\times_XY$ with $p+1$ factors, $f_p:Y_p\to X$, and $F_p=f_p^*F$. In the analytic topology of [[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]] the natural augmented derived Cech map is a quasi-isomorphism:
$$F\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}Rf_{p*}F_p.$$
Here totalization is the normalized or unnormalized alternating-face total supplied by the simplicial-derived construction. There is one fixed lower cochain bound; consequently its diagonals are finite in every degree. The claim commutes with arbitrary algebraic base change and coefficient morphisms. In particular $R\Gamma(X,F)\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_pR\Gamma(Y_p,F_p)$. Individual fibers of $f$ need not be cohomologically acyclic, connected, or smooth.

Fix an algebraically closed field $k$. The affine models used here are polynomial zero sets $Z\subseteq k^n$, including empty and reducible sets. Their closed subsets are common zero loci of polynomial families, relative to $Z$. Intersections combine equations, and finite unions use products of equations, so these are the closed sets of a topology.

For an open $U\subseteq Z$, let $\mathcal O_Z(U)$ consist of functions $U\to k$ locally equal to $a/b$ for polynomials $a,b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the chosen neighbourhood. Pointwise operations and restriction make these sets a sheaf of $k$-algebras: quotient expressions persist on restriction, and functions that agree locally glue uniquely with the same local quotient property. At a point z its stalk is the ring of germs of such functions. Evaluation at z maps it onto k, with kernel the germs vanishing at z. A germ nonzero at z is invertible: shrink to where its numerator and denominator are both nonzero and interchange them. Thus the kernel is the unique maximal ideal. These affine models are locally ringed spaces in the sense of [[def-locally-ringed-space]], with residue fields canonically k.

A **classical algebraic prevariety** over k is a quasi-compact locally ringed space with a structure sheaf of k-algebras, covered by open subspaces isomorphic over k to these affine models. Here quasi-compact means every open cover has a finite subcover. Equivalently it admits a finite affine-model cover. To justify the converse, each affine model is quasi-compact: polynomial principal opens $D_Z(h)=\{z:h(z)\ne0\}$ form a basis. Given an open cover, take all h whose principal opens lie in a member. Their principal opens cover Z. The ideal generated by these h in $k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$ is finitely generated by [[thm-hilbert-basis-theorem]], iterated from the field k. Express finitely many generators using finitely many of the original h. Those finitely many h have the same common zero locus as the whole ideal, hence their principal opens still cover Z and yield a finite subcover. The empty model has the empty subcover. A finite union of quasi-compact subspaces is quasi-compact.

A map is **regular** when it is a morphism of locally ringed spaces as in [[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]] whose sheaf maps respect k. For these function sheaves its sheaf map is necessarily pullback of functions: the local stalk map induces a k-map between residue fields k, hence the identity, so the value of a pulled-back section at x is its value at the image of x. Conversely, continuous pullback of local regular functions gives a local stalk map because a function vanishing at the image vanishes after pullback.

Regularity can therefore be checked on affine charts: near every source point choose a target affine chart containing its image and an open neighbourhood in a source affine chart mapped into it; the target coordinate functions must pull back to locally polynomial quotients. This condition also implies continuity. Indeed zero sets of locally polynomial quotients are locally polynomial zero sets, hence closed; pulling back polynomial equations consequently gives closed sets. Substitution then pulls every local quotient on the target back to a local quotient on the source, using this continuity to restrict to its domain and its nonvanishing denominator. Thus the chart condition and the locally ringed-space definition agree.

A prevariety is **separated** when the equalizer of every pair of regular maps into it, from any classical prevariety, is closed. A **classical algebraic variety** is a separated prevariety. Here varieties may be reducible or empty; an **irreducible classical variety** is nonempty and irreducible in the sense of [[def-irreducible-topological-space-and-subset]]. These definitions and the local verifications above use no Axiom of Choice.

Let $X$ be a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]: a separated
quasi-compact locally ringed space over $\mathbb C$ with a finite cover by
affine models $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the morphisms being the regular maps,
i.e. the morphisms of locally ringed spaces over $\mathbb C$
([[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]]).

(a) **Analytic topology.** An affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ carries the
subspace topology of the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb C^n$
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]],
[[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). If $Z_1,Z_2\subseteq X$ are affine
models and $\varphi:Z_1\to Z_2$ is the structure-sheaf isomorphism, then on
$Z_1\cap Z_2$ the maps $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are given locally by
polynomial quotient functions
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]) and are
therefore continuous for the Euclidean topologies: polynomial functions are
continuous, and a quotient is continuous wherever its denominator does not
vanish ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]],
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). Hence the topologies transported
from the two affine models agree on the overlap, so the affine-model topologies
glue to a unique topology on the underlying set of $X$
([[def-topological-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]): the **analytic
topology** of $X$. Every regular map of complex classical varieties is
continuous for the analytic topologies, by the same local description
([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and the analytic topology refines the Zariski
topology because polynomial zero sets are Euclidean closed. Whenever a complex
algebraic variety is used as a topological space below it carries the analytic
topology, and each subvariety carries the subspace topology.

(b) **Smooth points.** Let $S$ be a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ and let
$x\in S$. The point $x$ is a **smooth point of $S$** if its algebraic local ring
$\mathcal O_{S,x}$ is a regular local ring: a nonzero Noetherian local ring
whose maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_x$ satisfies
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2)=\dim\mathcal O_{S,x}$
([[def-embedding-dimension-and-regular-local-ring]]). The residue field at a
classical complex point is $\mathbb C$. The variety $S$ is **smooth** if every
point is smooth. This intrinsic algebraic condition does not require a Zariski
neighbourhood to be algebraically isomorphic to an open subset of affine space.

(c) **Finite smooth algebraic stratifications.** A **finite smooth algebraic
stratification with the frontier condition** of $X$ is a finite decomposition
$X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty connected
locally closed subsets $S_\alpha\subseteq X$ — the **strata** — such that each
$S_\alpha$, with its reduced induced algebraic structure, is a smooth algebraic
subvariety of $X$; and such that for every $\alpha$ the closure
$\overline{S_\alpha}$ of $S_\alpha$ in $X$ is a union of strata. The latter is
the **frontier condition**: the frontier
$\overline{S_\alpha}\setminus S_\alpha$ of every stratum is a union of strata
([[def-connected-space]], [[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]).

**The induced structure is the polynomial-quotient function sheaf, not a
restriction of $\mathcal O_X$.** A locally closed $S\subseteq X$ is, locally
inside an affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the set of points with $h\neq0$
and $f_1=\dots=f_r=0$ for polynomials $h,f_1,\dots,f_r$ on $Z$
([[def-constructible-subset-variety]],
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]); the map
$z\mapsto(z,1/h(z))$ identifies it with the affine model
$\{(z,t):th(z)=1,\ f_1(z)=\dots=f_r(z)=0\}\subseteq\mathbb C^{n+1}$, and its
**reduced induced structure sheaf** is the one transported along this
identification: locally functions of the form $a/b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the
set. The ambient restriction $\mathcal O_X|_S$ is not used, since already at the
origin of the affine line the ambient stalk is the local ring of the line while
the stalk of the reduced point is $\mathbb C$. An open subset of an affine model
is a union of principal open subsets, and each principal open subset is again an
affine model, so every locally closed subvariety of $X$ is a classical variety
for the induced structure sheaf. No existence theorem for stratifications, no
common-refinement theorem and no choice principle is asserted: nothing is
selected, and all cited suppliers are choice-free.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

**A point outside $X$, named rather than assumed.** Put

$$\infty \;:=\; \{\, y \in X : y \notin y \,\},$$

a set by Separation. Then $\infty \notin X$: were $\infty \in X$, the defining
condition applied to $\infty$ itself would give
$\infty \in \infty \iff \infty \notin \infty$. So no hypothesis about $X$ is
needed to obtain a point outside it, and the construction below is available for
every space.

**The space.** Put $X^{*} := X \cup \{\infty\}$ and

$$\mathcal{T}^{*} \;:=\; \mathcal{T} \;\cup\; \{\, X^{*} \setminus C \;:\; C \subseteq X,\ C \text{ closed in } X \text{ and a compact subset of } X \,\} .$$

The pair $(X^{*}, \mathcal{T}^{*})$ is the **one-point compactification**, or
**Alexandroff compactification**, of $X$. Members of $\mathcal{T}$ are said to be
of the **first kind** and the sets $X^{*} \setminus C$ of the **second kind**; a
set of the second kind is exactly an open set of $\mathcal{T}^{*}$ containing
$\infty$, since a member of $\mathcal{T}$ is a subset of $X$, and the set $C$ is
recovered from it as $C = X^{*} \setminus (X^{*} \setminus C)$.

**$\mathcal{T}^{*}$ is a topology on $X^{*}$, and this is discharged here.**
Throughout, "closed" and "compact" without qualification mean closed in $X$ and a
compact subset of $X$ ([[def-compact-space]]); two facts about such sets are used
and both are [[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]: a subset of a
compact $C$ that is closed in $X$ is closed in the subspace $C$
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]) and hence compact, and a union of two compact
subsets is compact.

*(T1).* $\varnothing \in \mathcal{T}$, and $X^{*} = X^{*} \setminus \varnothing$
is of the second kind, $\varnothing$ being closed in $X$ and compact.

*(T2).* Let $\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{T}^{*}$, let $\mathcal{S}_1$ be the
members of $\mathcal{S}$ lying in $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{S}_2$ the rest, so
that every member of $\mathcal{S}_2$ is of the second kind. If
$\mathcal{S}_2 = \varnothing$ then $\bigcup \mathcal{S} = \bigcup \mathcal{S}_1$
lies in $\mathcal{T}$ by (T2) in $X$. Otherwise put
$U := \bigcup \mathcal{S}_1 \in \mathcal{T}$ and
$\mathcal{D} := \{\, X^{*} \setminus O : O \in \mathcal{S}_2 \,\}$, a nonempty
family of closed compact subsets of $X$, and $C_0 := \bigcap \mathcal{D}$. Then
$C_0$ is closed by (C2) of [[def-topological-space]], and it is a closed subset of
any one member of $\mathcal{D}$, hence compact. Now

$$\bigcup \mathcal{S} \;=\; U \cup (X^{*} \setminus C_0) \;=\; X^{*} \setminus (C_0 \setminus U),$$

and $C_0 \setminus U = C_0 \cap (X \setminus U)$ is closed in $X$ and a subset of
the compact $C_0$, hence compact; so $\bigcup \mathcal{S}$ is of the second kind.

*(T3).* For $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ the intersection lies in $\mathcal{T}$ by (T3)
in $X$. For two sets of the second kind,
$(X^{*} \setminus C) \cap (X^{*} \setminus D) = X^{*} \setminus (C \cup D)$, and
$C \cup D$ is closed in $X$ and compact as a union of two compact subsets. For one
of each, $\infty \notin U$ gives
$U \cap (X^{*} \setminus C) = U \cap (X \setminus C)$, an intersection of two
members of $\mathcal{T}$.

**Why the compact sets are also required to be closed.** The complement of a
compact set that is not closed in $X$ would not make $\infty$'s neighbourhoods
behave: the union computation in (T2) uses that an intersection of the discarded
sets is again closed, and the intersection of arbitrary compact subsets of a
non-Hausdorff space need not be compact. When $X$ is Hausdorff every compact
subset is closed ([[thm-compact-subset-of-a-hausdorff-space-is-closed]]) and the
two descriptions agree, which is why many texts state the definition without the
word "closed" and silently assume the Hausdorff case.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$(X^{*}, \mathcal{T}^{*})$ be its one-point compactification, with added point
$\infty$ ([[def-one-point-compactification]]). Then:

1. **$X^{*}$ is compact** ([[def-compact-space]]).
2. **$X$ is an open subspace of $X^{*}$**: $X \in \mathcal{T}^{*}$, and the
   subspace topology that $X$ inherits from $X^{*}$
   ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]) is $\mathcal{T}$ itself.
3. **$X$ is dense in $X^{*}$** ([[def-dense-top]]) **if and only if $X$ is not
   compact.**
4. **$X^{*}$ is Hausdorff** ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) **if and only if $X$ is
   locally compact** ([[def-locally-compact-space]]) **and Hausdorff.**

In particular, a locally compact Hausdorff space is an open subspace of a compact
Hausdorff space, which is the reason the construction is made. **No choice
principle is used**: the only cover thinned below is thinned by the indexed form
of [[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], which returns its own indices.

Let
$$S^2:=\{(x,y,t)\in\mathbb R^3:x^2+y^2+t^2=1\}.$$
Define
$$\Sigma(z)=\left(\frac{2\operatorname{Re}z}{1+|z|^2},\ \frac{2\operatorname{Im}z}{1+|z|^2},\ \frac{|z|^2-1}{1+|z|^2}\right)\qquad(z\in\mathbb C)$$
and $\Sigma(\infty)=(0,0,1)$. Then $\Sigma:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to S^2$ is a
homeomorphism, with inverse
$$\Pi(x,y,t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x+iy}{1-t},&(x,y,t)\neq(0,0,1),\\ \infty,&(x,y,t)=(0,0,1).\end{cases}$$

If $f:X\to Y$ is a homotopy equivalence, then for every $n\geq 0$ and every
abelian group $G$ the induced map
$$H_n(f_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(Y;G)$$
is an isomorphism.

For $n\ge1$, $\widetilde H_k(S^n;G)$ is $G$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
For $S^0$, $\widetilde H_0(S^0;G)\cong G$ and all other reduced groups vanish.
Thus $H_0(S^n;G)\cong G$ for $n\ge1$, whereas
$H_0(S^0;G)\cong G\oplus G$.

Assume AC. For every field $k$, every space $X$, and $n\ge0$, evaluation gives a natural $k$-linear isomorphism
$$H^n(X;k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_k(H_n(X;k),k).$$
There is no finite-dimensional hypothesis. The right side is the full algebraic dual.

A morphism $f:X\to Y$ of classical varieties is projective here if there is an integer $N\ge0$ and a factorization $X\hookrightarrow Y\times\mathbf P_k^N\to Y$ in which the first map is a closed immersion and the second is projection. The product and its standard charts are supplied by [[lem-relative-projective-homogeneous-equations]]. A closed immersion in this classical setting is an isomorphism onto a reduced closed subvariety. Morphisms have the general locally ringed-space meaning of [[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]], checked on affine charts.

Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

Assume AC. Let $f:X\to Y$ be one morphism of reduced quasi-projective complex
algebraic varieties, and prescribe finitely many closed or locally closed
algebraic subsets in source and target. There exist finite smooth complex
algebraic Whitney (a),(b) stratifications with frontier on $X$ and $Y$
respecting all prescribed subsets, such that each source stratum maps
surjectively and smoothly onto one target stratum. A further finite algebraic
stratification may be prescribed and refined. The analytic strata are smooth
complex manifolds and the restrictions are smooth submersions. If $f$ is proper
in the analytic topology, in particular if it is a projective algebraic
morphism, the whole restriction $f^{-1}(T)\to T$ over any target stratum is
proper; no restriction of $f$ to a nonclosed individual source stratum is
asserted proper.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) having a neighbourhood basis of contractible open sets at
every point, and let $k$ be a field. Write $k_X$ for its constant sheaf. There
are natural isomorphisms
$$H^q(X,k_X)\cong H^q_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$$
in every degree, where the left side is derived cohomology in the category of
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces (computed with the functorial $k$-linear injective
resolutions supplied by
[[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]; compare
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). The same assertion holds on
every open subset of $X$. In particular a nonempty contractible space with this
local property has constant-sheaf cohomology $k$ in degree zero and zero
otherwise. This applies to every finite-polyhedral open star and to its
nonempty intersection with a closed simplex.
